short: Nobody knows who owns the broken automation
full: A workflow fails, but nobody knows who is responsible for fixing it.

short: The same workflow built in three tools
full: Different teams maintain separate automations for the same task.

short: AI tools bought before anyone checks access
full: A team buys an AI tool before checking which company data it needs to access.

short: No record of what the AI changed
full: We cannot trace which records an AI workflow edited or why it edited them.

short: Old employees still have access to our tools
full: People who left the company still have active accounts or permissions.

short: New AI tools. No plan to maintain them.
full: Teams launch AI workflows without assigning anyone to keep them working.

short: Hard to tell which tools are worth keeping
full: We pay for overlapping tools without a clear view of who uses them or what they save.

short: Failed automations disappear without an alert
full: A workflow stops running, but the team does not hear about the failure.

short: Two systems disagree on the same record
full: We have to investigate which system has the current information before we can act.

short: Testing AI changes takes too much manual work
full: Every change to an AI workflow needs repeated manual checks before we can trust it.

short: An AI retry creates duplicate records
full: Retrying a failed AI action adds a second record instead of safely finishing the first.

short: No easy way to stop a bad AI action
full: When an AI workflow starts making incorrect changes, stopping it takes too long.

short: Permissions are different in every tool
full: Keeping the right people and workflows connected requires separate access checks in each tool.

short: Sensitive data ends up in the wrong AI tool
full: People paste private company or customer information into tools that were not approved for it.

short: Every AI vendor needs another security review
full: Each new AI tool starts another round of questions about data, access and vendor controls.

short: No one checks whether the automation still works
full: A workflow keeps running after the business process changes, with no owner checking its output.

short: Hard to explain where an AI answer came from
full: We cannot trace an AI answer back to the source records it used.

short: An integration update breaks our field mappings
full: After a system update, information lands in the wrong fields or stops syncing.

short: The AI pilot has no clear measure of success
full: We launched a pilot without agreeing how to check whether it actually helps the team.

short: Support agents start every ticket from scratch
full: Agents have to rebuild the customer's history before they can respond to a new ticket.

short: Urgent support tickets wait in the wrong queue
full: A time-sensitive customer issue gets sent to a team that cannot resolve it.

short: Customers chase us for ticket updates
full: Customers have to ask for progress because nobody sends an update while their issue is open.

short: The same support issue keeps coming back
full: We close individual tickets without fixing the problem that keeps creating new ones.

short: Support answers depend on who takes the ticket
full: Agents give different answers to the same question because their guidance is inconsistent.

short: Old help articles keep getting sent to clients
full: Support replies link to guidance that no longer matches the product or policy.

short: Ticket handoffs lose the troubleshooting history
full: The next support team cannot see what has already been tried, so the customer repeats the steps.

short: Support managers review tickets one by one
full: Checking service quality means manually reading individual tickets with little help finding issues.

short: The support backlog hides the biggest problems
full: A long ticket queue makes it hard to spot the issues with the greatest customer impact.

short: No one owns the next step on an escalation
full: An escalated support issue passes between teams without a clear person responsible for moving it forward.

short: Customers get different answers in chat and email
full: Our support channels use different information when answering the same customer question.

short: Hard to tell which tickets need a specialist
full: Support agents spend too long deciding whether an issue needs a different team or expert.

short: Support quality checks miss repeat mistakes
full: Our ticket reviews do not reliably catch the same incorrect advice being sent to more customers.

short: Ticket summaries leave out the important detail
full: A summary misses the error, customer impact or troubleshooting step the next agent needs.

short: Support policies change. Saved replies don't.
full: Agents keep sending old saved replies after the relevant policy has changed.

short: One client problem becomes five separate tickets
full: We treat related tickets as separate issues and miss the full picture of the customer's problem.

short: Hard to explain why a ticket was prioritized
full: The team cannot see what made a ticket more urgent than other work in the queue.

short: Case evidence is spread across too many tools
full: Reviewers have to move between systems to assemble the records needed for one case.

short: Payment reviews pile up in a shared inbox
full: Payment cases arrive in an inbox with no reliable way to assign and track the next action.

short: Dispute deadlines get buried in the queue
full: The team spots a dispute too late to collect and submit the evidence before its deadline.

short: Reviewers disagree on the same kind of case
full: Similar cases receive different decisions because reviewers interpret the available evidence differently.

short: Hard to explain why a transaction was flagged
full: A reviewer sees a risk alert without enough detail to understand what triggered it.

short: Good customers get stuck in manual review
full: Legitimate customers wait too long while the team investigates a flagged transaction or account.

short: Rebuilding the case history takes longer than review
full: Finding prior decisions and customer records takes more time than assessing the current case.

short: Case handoffs lose the reason for escalation
full: A reviewer receives an escalated case without a clear explanation of what needs investigation.

short: Policy updates never reach the review checklist
full: The team keeps using an old checklist after the policy governing its decisions has changed.

short: Missing evidence only surfaces at final review
full: A case reaches the final reviewer before anyone notices that a required record is missing.

short: Too many alerts. Too few useful clues.
full: Reviewers receive large numbers of risk alerts that do not explain which evidence deserves attention.

short: Dispute evidence gets copied into every form
full: The team manually copies the same case records into multiple dispute documents or systems.

short: Case notes don't explain the final decision
full: The record says what was decided but leaves out the evidence and reasoning behind that decision.

short: Closed cases come back with the same questions
full: A finished case is reopened because the original review did not answer the questions clearly.

short: Payment records don't match across systems
full: The team must reconcile conflicting transaction details before it can finish a payment review.

short: Review queues hide overdue cases
full: Cases pass their review deadline without becoming visible to the person who can resolve them.

short: Fraud patterns are spotted one case too late
full: The team sees a recurring pattern only after several related cases have already been handled.

short: Too much time spent clearing false alarms
full: Reviewers repeatedly investigate alerts that turn out to have a straightforward, legitimate explanation.

short: Nobody knows who owns the disputed payment
full: A payment dispute moves between teams without a clear owner responsible for resolving it.

short: Risk reviewers can't find the current policy
full: Reviewers spend time searching for the policy version that applies to the case in front of them.

short: Case decisions are hard to audit later
full: Months after a decision, the team cannot easily reconstruct the records and reasoning used at the time.

short: Urgent cases look like every other case
full: The queue does not clearly distinguish cases that need immediate attention from routine reviews.

short: The case summary leaves out conflicting evidence
full: A summary presents one conclusion without showing the records that point to a different interpretation.

short: Asking customers twice for the same evidence
full: Different reviewers request documents that the customer has already supplied for the same case.

short: No feedback when a risk alert was wrong
full: The people maintaining our review rules do not hear which alerts reviewers found unhelpful or incorrect.

short: Client news gets noticed after the opportunity passes
full: We hear about a meaningful change at a client too late to start a useful conversation.

short: Executive moves get lost in the news feed
full: A key person changes jobs, but nobody connects the move to our client relationships.

short: Market alerts arrive without a next step
full: The team receives a relevant update without knowing who should act or what to do next.

short: Every partner keeps a separate client watchlist
full: People track the same clients independently, so useful changes and follow-ups stay scattered.

short: No clear owner for following up on client news
full: A meaningful client update is shared around the team, but nobody owns the response.

short: Relationship history is buried in old emails
full: Before contacting a client or prospect, we struggle to find the history of who knows whom.

short: Finding the real source behind a market claim
full: Research gets repeated without a reliable way to check where the original claim came from.

short: Weekly market briefs take days to assemble
full: The team spends too long collecting and checking sources before it can discuss the implications.

short: Important client changes disappear in long reports
full: A useful change is buried in a report that the relationship owner does not have time to read.

short: Research gets shared but never changes the plan
full: The team collects market insight without connecting it to an account, message or strategic decision.

short: Industry news isn't linked to the clients it affects
full: We spot a market change but do not identify which clients might need a conversation about it.

short: Warm introductions depend on someone's memory
full: We miss useful introductions because relationship connections are not easy to find or verify.

short: Client priorities changed. Our brief didn't.
full: We enter a client conversation using research that no longer reflects the client's situation.

short: Market summaries leave out the supporting evidence
full: A research summary makes a claim without the source or context needed to judge whether it is useful.
